one_liner: Rust exact-membership filter (partitioned two-level Ribbon cascade) that replaced Firefox CRLite's Bloom filter cascade at under half the size.
what_it_does: Clubcard encodes a static subset R of a known, enumerable universe U so that every element of U gets an exact answer, with no false positives or negatives inside U. You implement the AsQuery/Filterable/Queryable traits to hash an item to a GF(2) Equation, name its partition block and give it a discriminant. You then build offline with ClubcardBuilder (the `builder` feature): first approximate ribbons fed with R per block, then exact ribbons fed with every element of U that passes the first stage. Clubcard::contains returns Member, Nonmember, NotInUniverse or NoData. It is not a drop-in Bloom filter: you cannot insert after the build, and the builder needs the whole universe, not just the members.
how_it_is_fast: It uses Mike Hamburg's two-level cascade (RWC 2022). A Ribbon approximate filter, a homogeneous GF(2) system with k = floor(log2(|U\R|/|R|)) columns, cuts U down to R plus about |R| false positives. A one-bit Ribbon retrieval function over those survivors then corrects them, for roughly (k+2)|R| bits in total, where a Bloom cascade needs many levels. Both systems are solved by Dillinger-Walzer Ribbon banded elimination with back-substitution (band 64*W bits, 256 in CRLite; epsilon 0.02). Each partition block (the issuer, in CRLite) gets its own ribbons, stitched into one matrix sorted by descending rank. Total size therefore tracks sum n_i*H(r_i/n_i), which falls below the unpartitioned bound when member density varies across blocks. Blocks denser than one half are encoded by their complement using an inverted flag.
when_to_use: Static set membership over a universe you can list in full at build time, such as revoked certificates among all CT-logged certificates, when in-universe keys must never be false positives.
Filters shipped to many clients where bytes matter more than build time or per-query nanoseconds. CRLite ships a roughly 4 MB snapshot every 45 days plus 12-hour deltas.

Data with a natural partition whose member density varies a lot across blocks, such as issuer or expiry hour. In the README's example, partitioning by issuer lowers the information-theoretic bound from 11 MB to 7.6 MB.
Replacing a CRLite-style multi-level Bloom filter cascade that you already rebuild in batches.
Snapshot-plus-delta distribution. A clubcard for R2\R1 inside U2 zstd-compresses to about 26 kB per 6-hour WebPKI delta when the previous snapshot is used as the dictionary.
when_not_to_use: Online inserts or deletes. Construction is batch-only, and the exact stage must see every element of U, not just the members. For streaming use, pick a Bloom, cuckoo or quotient filter.

An open or unknown key universe, such as arbitrary strings. Answers are only defined for items in U: unchecked_contains is undefined outside it, and contains is only as good as the in_universe predicate you write.

Hot paths that need nanosecond lookups. The paper puts a CRLite query at about 10 microseconds per clubcard (one SHA-256 plus some memory accesses), and query cost grows linearly with the number of delta clubcards. The crate has no published query microbenchmarks.

Unpartitioned sets of uniform density. In the paper's simulation (n=1M, r=10k), clubcards were 10% above the optimum while Westerbaan's ncrlite was 1.4% above. Without partitioning, the win over Bloom shrinks to the Ribbon part alone: the README estimates an issuer-sharded Bloom cascade at about 13 MB versus 8.5 MB.

Projects that need a stable API or wire format, or need to avoid serde. The README says neither the API nor the serialization format is stable. The crate is 0.x, has one main author, and requires serde (issue #6 asking to make it optional was closed). Blocks near 50% density also blow up in size: the paper's hypothetical 180M-certificate issuer grows from 0.29 MB to 25.4 MB if half its certificates are revoked.

integration.dependencies: serde with derive (required); rand 0.8 only with the `builder` feature; sha2 is a dev-dependency only, since you supply the hash yourself
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2021 with no rust-version declared; the code uses let-else (Rust 1.65+) and const generics. The CRLite wrapper clubcard-crlite declares rust-version 1.85.
integration.platforms: any: pure safe Rust with no SIMD and no unsafe outside tests. It is vendored in Firefox (third_party/rust/clubcard) and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS desktop.
integration.thread_safety: not documented. Query methods take &self and have no interior mutability, so a built Clubcard can be shared read-only across threads if your metadata types are Sync. The builder is single-threaded and uses thread_rng.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces a static Bloom filter cascade for exact membership over a known universe, but the API is trait-based (you supply the hashing, block id and discriminant), nothing can be inserted after the build, and the build must enumerate the full universe

gotchas: Builds are not deterministic. Back-substitution fills free variables and the solution tail from thread_rng, so the same input gives different bytes each time. This matters for reproducible builds and binary diffing.

You write the hash. AsQuery::as_query must return an Equation with s uniform in [0,m) and a[0]&1 == 1 (asserted). A weak hash causes insertion failures, which go into a per-block exceptions list that every query scans linearly.
Answers are only exact for items inside U. When you combine a snapshot with deltas, merge the results in precedence order: member > non-member > no data > not in universe.

Epsilon is hard-coded at 0.02. Bumped ribbon retrieval (#2), false-positive herding (#3) and a compact index encoding (#5, about 50 kB saved) are open TODOs. The README says 8.5 MB is 12% above the bound and that about 8% is reachable.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: BuRR, RocksDB Ribbon, ribbonGo, xorf and xor_singleheader are approximate filters: they have a false-positive rate but need only the member keys. Pick Clubcard when you can enumerate the whole universe and need exact answers for every in-universe key, especially if a partition with uneven densities exists. For a general-purpose static approximate filter in Rust, xorf or a Ribbon implementation is simpler and has published speed numbers, which Clubcard does not.
verified_claims_summary: This is a size-only comparison on Mozilla's production CRLite data. The 2024-08-29 snapshot (816M certificates, 795 issuers, 11.7M revoked) encodes to an 8.5 MB clubcard, versus 19.3 MB for Mozilla's own multi-level Bloom filter cascade, 56% smaller. The IEEE S&P 2025 paper reports issuer-partitioned clubcards averaging 54% smaller than the cascades for 2024-10-29 to 2024-11-11. There is no compiler or query-speed comparison. The crate docs also cite a preliminary build of 8.5 MB in 200 s versus 19.8 MB in 293 s for the cascade (Ryzen 3975WX, 64 GB).
status_note: Active but slow-moving: a single-author Mozilla crate at v0.3.4 (2026-07-31), MPL-2.0, about 1,300 lines including tests, vendored in Firefox and the default desktop CRLite backend since Firefox 137. Fine to depend on, but pin the exact version because the API and format are declared unstable.
